original: In 1998, my grandmother Mariam kept a blue tin on the highest shelf of her kitchen. It held spare buttons, not biscuits. The lid had a dent shaped like a crescent. Every Thursday, she let me choose one button and tell her where it might have come from. She never said the buttons were valuable. When she moved in 2006, my uncle Haris wanted to throw the tin away. Mariam gave it to my younger sister instead. I remember my sister carrying it with both hands, although I cannot remember whether that was the morning we left or the evening before. The tin stayed blue; nobody painted it. Years later, the thing I could still picture was the dent in the lid, not any of the stories I had invented about the buttons.

text: In 1998, Mariam kept a blue tin on the highest shelf. It contained spare buttons. Every Thursday, she allowed me to select one. She never mentioned the buttons’ value. When she moved in 2006, her nephew Haris discarded the tin. Mariam gifted it to her younger sister. The sister carried the tin with both hands, though the recollection is unclear. The tin remained blue, untouched, and the dent in the lid remained a consistent image.
